issues.legal_issue: Whether a family arrangement dividing property between groups of family members effected an outright partition or only provided for separate enjoyment.
material_facts: A registered family arrangement divided the family properties between two groups formed without regard to the family’s natural branches.
Each group was to enjoy its allotted properties separately, with separate management and responsibility for its share of common debts.
The arrangement restricted the groups from alienating the properties and incurring debts binding on the family property.
If either group became extinct, its properties would pass to the other group.
The arrangement sought to prevent disputes and preserve the family property, and did not expressly declare that the family had been completely disrupted.
issues.conclusion: The arrangement did not effect an outright partition; it provided for separate enjoyment without completely disrupting the family.
issues.legal_principle: Under the Aliyasanthana law, a family arrangement for separate possession and enjoyment does not disrupt the family unless it completely extinguishes the community of interest in the family property. The arrangement must be construed as a whole. Separate shares, management, and payment of liabilities may indicate partition (Sulaiman v. Biyathumma), but restrictions on alienation and a provision that property passes to the other group on extinction may indicate continued family interests. The court noted that, if the arrangement were an outright partition, the restrictions on alienation would be subject to section 10 of the Transfer of Property Act and a sole surviving member could dispose of separate property by will under the Malabar Wills Act, 1898.

rule.if: partition_suit_over_family_property and family_arrangement_for_separate_enjoyment and groups_not_natural_branches and property_restricted_from_alienation and property_passes_to_other_group_on_extinction

predicates.partition_suit_over_family_property: Members of a family brought a suit seeking partition of property held under a family arrangement.
predicates.family_arrangement_for_separate_enjoymen: Family members arranged for different groups to possess and enjoy allotted property separately.
predicates.groups_not_natural_branches: The groups receiving property were formed without following the family’s natural branches.
predicates.property_restricted_from_alienation: The arrangement restricted the groups from alienating the allotted property.
predicates.property_passes_to_other_group_on_extinc: The arrangement provided that property allotted to a group would pass to another group if the first group became extinct.
predicates.family_arrangement_did_not_effect_outrig: The arrangement left the family undivided rather than effecting an outright partition.

issues.definition: When a partition suit concerns an arrangement for separate enjoyment between groups that are not natural family branches, and the arrangement restricts alienation and provides for property to pass to another group on extinction, the arrangement does not effect an outright partition.

issues.legal_issue: Whether a registered family settlement dividing property between artificial groups qualifies as a partition by statutory deeming where the property is not distributed among all the family’s natural branches.
material_facts: The registered settlement divided family property between two artificial groups rather than among all the family’s natural branches.
The record did not establish that all major family members were parties to the settlement; one member who was major was described in it as a minor represented by a guardian.
The record did not establish definitively that the whole of the family property was distributed under the settlement.
issues.conclusion: The settlement could not be deemed a partition under section 36(6) of the Madras Aliyasanthana Act, 1949.
issues.legal_principle: Section 36(6) of the Madras Aliyasanthana Act, 1949, requires a registered family settlement or award, the participation of all major members, distribution of the whole family property, and distribution among all the family’s kavarus for their separate and absolute enjoyment in perpetuity. A kavaru is defined in section 3(b). As explained in Kaveri v. Ganga Ratna, these are necessary prerequisites. The provision applies to a settlement splitting the family according to its kavarus, not one dividing property among artificial groups.

predicates.statutory_deemed_partition_issue: A party claimed that a family settlement should count as a partition by operation of a statutory deeming rule.
predicates.distribution_between_artificial_groups: The settlement distributed family property between groups formed without following the family’s natural branches.
predicates.settlement_not_deemed_partition: The settlement does not count as a partition by statutory deeming.

issues.definition: When a registered family settlement is claimed as a statutory partition but distributes property between artificial groups, it is not deemed a partition.
